Things that help me:

  1. Know the genre. Study the popular stories, but obviously do not copy them. Get an idea for the descriptive details the readers like.

  2. When I come up with an idea, I write it. Like a sculpture, I rough-in the story from start to finish with no editing or going back to change something (unless it's important) then I go back over it and add details like colors of dresses, what a room looks like or other background info, etc.

  3. Make sure your sex scenes turn you on. Seriously, like write them in such a manner that you feel the need to masturbate before you're half done writing it (but finish the scene first). I wrote a solo sex scene where the spirit explores the body it had just possessed that and had a difficult time keeping my hands out of my pants. The first M/F sex was modeled after an actual event in my life (minus the possession) that I still masturbate to many years later. I tell you this with honesty and not blushing because it helps the writing.

  4. Characters should have their own "voice." A macho male would never use "weensy" in a sentence unless he was being sarcastic and a stereotypical feminine character would never say "I sucked his Johnson with fervor."

  5. Avoid words ending in -ly. You're still going to use them, but anytime you can rephrase a sentence without an -ly adverb, do so. A noun also does not need to be flourished with two or three adjectives.

  6. Read Stephen King's On Writing.

  7. Have fun with it. The more you enjoy writing it, the better it's going to turn out.

  8. Pet names for body parts can turn off readers. Use "cock/dick, clit and ass" not "pole/member, flower, booty." (At least for most erotica. If you're going for a much more romantic than fucking style, this does not apply.)

  9. Even if it's a short story, follow a three act structure and the "call to adventure" trope as closely as you can. The "adventure" can be as simple as "I need to get laid" or "Oh, the UPS guy is here!"

  10. Take risks. Accept negative criticism and learn your weaknesses from that.

  11. Don't edit until the story is done. Less is more, so when you can go back, subtract what isn't needed.

  12. Have a fantasy you'd never do/could do in real life? Let your characters! I'd never go to a gloryhole, but my characters do.

That's about all I can think of for now, and I wish you the best of luck. I'll send you a link or copy of my stories when I'm finished editing them if you'd like. YYYeeeaaahhh... this article is biased in every way, shape, and form. So much bullshit.

I'll give you one:

The Fairness Doctrine was repealed in 1987 by the FCC. Reagan had staffed the FCC with prominent media businessmen who were intent on slashing government regulations… the equivalent of letting the fox guard the chicken coop.

That's pure bias. The fairness doctrine was the fox guarding the chicken coop. Putting an entity with a monopoly on force 100% in charge of determining what can and can't be said is always-- always-- a bad idea, and anyone who says differently is gaining money or power off the transaction.

Pure bias?

Was "The Fairness Doctrine was repealed in 1987 by the FCC"? Is this a fact? Is there some other closely-related fact missing here that would say otherwise?

The fox here is the media executives, the chicken coup is media regulation. The example of the fox guarding it is the repeal of the fairness doctrine. This is quite standard analysis and the example is very specific. Could this have been said without the fox line even though it accurately characterized the situation? Sure. Conclusion: slight language bias.

Now, let's see some serious bias.

Putting an entity with a monopoly on force

  1. Incorrect statement. Nobody has a monopoly on force. The ability to use force varies.

  2. Very broad and vague generalization. For example, if government has a monopoly on force, isn't this being used to protect property ownership rights too?

100% in charge of determining what can and can't be said

Gross exaggeration. Fairness doctrine only said that, in certain situations, an alternative view must be presented. It did not say at all what could be said or not said, and it surely did not pick the speakers. Nearly all of TV broadcast was completely free of fairness doctrine requirements.
